figures.label: S1
figures.caption: Fig. S1. Schematic illustration of composite chalcogen cathodes prepared by ultrahigh-speed and conventional mixing. The conventional approaches using low-speed mixing of chalcogen cathode, solid-state electrolyte, and conductive carbon resulted in the formation of voids and poor solid/solid contact inside the resultant composite chalcogen cathodes, leading to poor ion transport, severe reaction heterogeneity, and contact loss upon cycling. By contrast, during ultrahigh-speed mixing, the localized heating striking and shearing fracturing force induce a mechanochemical reaction, leading to the segregation of nanosized lithium halides from bulk halogen-containing solid-state electrolytes and subsequent deposition onto the interface with chalcogen cathode particles. figures.label: S3
figures.caption: Fig. S3. Summary of sulfur utilization in the reported composite S cathodes prepared by different mixing speeds. References include studies on composite sulfur cathodes incorporating both sulfur-impregnated carbon structures and raw sulfur cycled at room temperature (1, 12, 13, 20, 22, 24, 43-59, 61-66). Note that the sulfur utilization reported in studies utilizing sulfide solid electrolytes may include extra capacity contributed by the redox reactions of the sulfides themselves. As shown, the Фs of the UHS-mixed composite S cathode was significantly increased compared to those using low speed, highlighting the crucial role of halide segregation in promoting the reaction kinetics of composite S cathodes.

figures.caption: Fig. S7. Cryo-TEM setup and sensitivity of argyrodite Li6PS5Cl solid electrolyte. (A, B) E- beam damage and air sensitivity of Li6PS5Cl. Room-temperature TEM (RT-TEM) has proven ineffective for imaging sulfide solid-state electrolytes due to their extreme vulnerability to e-beam damage, which is an order of magnitude greater than that of lithium metal (31). figures.caption: Fig. S8. Cryo-TEM images of argyrodite Li6PS5Cl under low e-beam dose at varying exposure times. Achieving high-resolution, high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) images while minimizing e-beam damage requires balancing the e-beam dose rate and exposure time under cryogenic conditions. Although longer exposure times improve the SNR, they can also cause sample drift. Lowering the e-beam dose rate helps reduce radiolysis and knock-on damage, which are the primary causes of structural changes in sensitive materials. A careful balance between the e-beam dose rate and exposure time is essential to maintain a high SNR without causing excessive damage. figures.label: S9
figures.caption: Fig. S9. In situ observation of argyrodite Li6PS5Cl. (A) Time-series TEM images at room temperature at 3.87 e– Å–2 s–1. (B) Time-series STEM images at room temperature at 0.25 nA. (C) Time-series TEM images at the cryogenic condition at 3.87 e– Å–2 s–1. In cryo-TEM, e-beam damage is influenced by both the dose rate (the number of electrons hitting a sample area per unit time) and the accumulated dose (total exposure during imaging). To assess the effect of accumulated dose on argyrodite Li6PS5Cl, in situ observations were conducted using bright-field and dark-field (DF) TEM, comparing room temperature and cryogenic conditions. In RT-TEM, Li6PS5Cl showed significant structural changes, including volume expansion, shrinkage, and pore formation, during a 107.5 s observation at a dose rate of 3.87 e– Å–2 s–1. Similar damage was confirmed in DF-STEM with a screen current of 0.25 nA over 97 s.

(C) S-L2,3 and Cl-L2,3 edges EELS spectra of selected regions #9/#10/#11 in (A) and (B). Ideally, elemental sulfur (S0) in the composite sulfur cathode, which exhibits molecular bonding, and sulfide ions (Sn–) from the LPSCl solid electrolyte, which exhibit ionic bonding, should display distinct EELS features due to their differences in valence state and bonding environments. figures.label: S13
figures.caption: Fig. S13. In situ SXRD patterns during heating of a hand-mixed mixture of elemental sulfur, carbon (Ketjenblack, C45), and Li6PS5Cl. To investigate the influence of the heating striking force, a composite sulfur cathode mixture was hand-grounded prior to the in situ heating experiment. The SXRD patterns showed that the crystalline peaks of elemental sulfur disappeared at about 100 °C, indicating the transition to an amorphous state after heating. Crystalline LiCl formation started to appear at about 200 °C, while nanocrystalline LiCl could form at a temperature below 200 °C by the localized heat during ultrahigh-speed mixing.

figures.caption: Fig. S15. Effect of heat treatment on the composite S cathode. (A) HAADF-STEM and bright field (BF)-STEM images, along with EDS elemental mapping of the hand-mixed composite S/LPSCl/C cathode without heat treatment. (B) HAADF-STEM and BF-STEM images along with EDS elemental mapping of the hand-mixed composite S/LPSCl/C cathode after heating at 145 °C for 3 h. (C) Comparison of normalized EDS spectra for P, S, and Cl elements in (A, #1) and (B, #2). The unheated S/LPSCl/C cathode shows a uniform distribution of P, S, and Cl elements, while the heated sample exhibits clear Cl segregation. The Cl peak intensity in the heated sample significantly increases relative to P, indicating an atomic ratio shift from the original 1:1 due to Cl segregation.

figures.caption: Fig. S36. (A) Ionic conductivities of Li6PS5Cl after different processing conditions. (B) Linear fits of peak current of composite sulfur cathodes processed under different conditions, as a function of scan rates. The ionic conductivities of the pristine Li6PS5Cl and Li6PS5Cl processed at 2000 rpm for 1 h, 5 h, and 10 h in (A) were 0.44, 0.11, 0.01, and 0.002 mS cm–1, respectively.
